mainEntity.name: Is HIV a barrier to getting dental implants?

acceptedAnswer.text: HIV is not automatically a barrier to dental implants. Current clinical evidence suggests that people living with HIV whose condition is well-managed through antiretroviral therapy may be suitable candidates for implant treatment. The key factors include immune function, viral load, overall oral health, and the absence of active infection. A thorough clinical assessment is required before any decision about suitability can be made, and no outcomes can be guaranteed without examination.

mainEntity.name: What CD4 count is generally considered safe for dental implant surgery?

acceptedAnswer.text: Published research and clinical guidance commonly reference a CD4 count above 200 cells/mm³ as a threshold associated with more favourable conditions for surgical procedures, including dental implants. However, this figure alone does not determine suitability. Your dental team will consider the full picture of your health, including viral load, medication, and oral health status. Decisions should always be made in consultation with both your dentist and your HIV specialist.

mainEntity.name: Will my dental team need to know about my HIV status?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Sharing your HIV status with your dental team is important for your safety and to enable appropriate clinical care. Your dental team is bound by strict confidentiality obligations and anti-discrimination duties. Knowing your medical history — including your current treatment and health status — allows your clinician to plan your care responsibly, coordinate with your other healthcare providers, and adapt the procedure appropriately to minimise risk and support healing.

mainEntity.name: Can antiretroviral medications affect dental implant treatment?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some antiretroviral medications may have implications for dental treatment, including effects on bone metabolism, healing, and interactions with anaesthetic agents or antibiotics used during or after implant surgery. It is important to provide your dental team with a full and up-to-date list of all medications you are taking. Your dentist may liaise with your HIV specialist to ensure that your treatment plan is safe, coordinated, and appropriate for your specific medical circumstances.

mainEntity.name: How do I prepare for a dental implant consultation if I am living with HIV?

acceptedAnswer.text: Preparation for an implant consultation involves gathering relevant medical information, including your most recent CD4 count and viral load results, a current list of your medications, and the contact details of your HIV consultant or GP. You should also be prepared to discuss your oral health history, any recent changes in your mouth, and your general health background. Being open with your dental team enables them to provide you with the most informed and personalised assessment possible.

mainEntity.name: Are there alternatives to dental implants for people living with HIV?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. If dental implants are not considered suitable following assessment, or if you prefer to explore other options, alternatives such as dental bridges or removable partial or full dentures may be discussed. Each option carries its own considerations in terms of longevity, aesthetics, function, and maintenance. Your dental team will help you understand which solutions may be appropriate for your individual needs and circumstances.
